newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Nuclear handover only while Yeltsin in surgery - TV.
newsitem.headline: Nuclear handover only while Yeltsin in surgery - TV.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin may hand over Russia's "nuclear button" to his prime minister only for as long as he is unconscious during heart surgery, NTV commercial television said on Sunday.

With a few weeks to go before Yeltsin's operation, NTV's Itogi programme disclosed what it said were hitherto secret details about the codes for launching missiles and the portable communications centre to enable them.

"We have learnt from Kremlin sources that just before the the operation starts the president will sign a decree handing over the 'nuclear button' to Viktor Chernomyrdin for a very short period of time," correspondent Vadim Glusker said.
"Immediately after the operation, when the doctors take the president out of the anaesthetic, he will sign a new decree taking back control of the 'nuclear button'," he added.

There has been speculation about who will control Russian nuclear forces when the 65-year-old leader is in the operating theatre. Doctors say Yeltsin needs a bypass operation to increase the flow of blood.
Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said last week that Yeltsin was considering different options but gave no clue as to what the final option could be.
Under the constitution the prime minister takes over if the president is not capable of carrying out his powers further.
A senior parliament member, Alexei Arbatov, told Itogi that the "nuclear button" was the first link in a chain of commands ending in cruise computers on board nuclear missiles.

"The 'nuclear button'...transmits presidential sanction for a use of nuclear weapons to command centres where general staff officers are on duty around the clock," said Arbatov, a leading expert in national security issues who has close ties with the Kremlin establishment.
"On receiving a coded signal officers...using appropriate codes determine that it was president, not someone else, who had sent it."
When the authenticity of the presidential message is confirmed, duty officers open safe boxes with their own codes and send them to missile launching pads and nuclear submarines.
"Then the codes are installed (into cruise computers), launch keys are turned and the missiles blast off," he said.
Glusker said that around 30 people are involved in handling the 'nuclear button' network run jointly by the defence ministry and secret services.

"Details change all the time but not the man who carries the case with the 'nuclear button'," Glusker said. "If you want to see him look out for an officer in black navy uniform following the president like a shadow wherever he goes."
He said the distinctive navy uniform had been chosen to make it easy for Yeltsin to distinguish the officer among his entourage should the need arise.
Arbatov said the defence minister had a similar 'nuclear button' but the president did not need to coordinate his orders with the military chief.
"The order of the first (president) does not need a confirmation by the second," Arbatov said.
He did not make clear whether the defence minister would need the president's authorisation to use his 'nuclear button'.
